Proteomic and Metabolomic Characterization of COVID-19 Patient Sera

Assignment 1 – Data Wrangling & Exploratory Data Analysis

Ramona Maria Walch (ramonamaria.walch01@estudiant.upf.edu)

20 March 2026

This practical focuses on data wrangling, exploratory data analysis, visualization, and critical comparison with published results using real biomedical data.

We will work with the publication Proteomic and Metabolomic Characterization of COVID-19 Patient Sera

1 Introduction

This report analyzes the dataset from Shen et al. (2020), comprising 118 individuals across four groups (Healthy Controls, Non-COVID-19, Non-severe, Severe COVID-19). The analysis covers data wrangling with MICE imputation, reproduction of Table 1 and Supplementary Figure 1, outlier handling via log-transformation, and hierarchical clustering for patient stratification.

2.2 Discussion of Discrepancies

Results closely match the published Table 1: age (Severe median 55 vs. Non-severe 43 years), sex distribution (65% male), and time metrics are faithfully reproduced. Minor deviations in group counts likely reflect MICE imputation.

Summary of EDA Findings

Age varied significantly by group (ANOVA: F=5.99, p<0.001), with Severe patients notably older (median 55 [IQR 47–64] years) than Non-severe (43 [36–51] years). BMI showed no significant group difference (F=1.90, p=0.134). Sex distribution was consistent across groups (65% male, 35% female). Missing data (~24% biomarkers, ~7% BMI) was handled transparently in downstream analyses.

3 Exercise 2

3.1 Exercise 2.1

Reproduce Supplementary Figure 1 using the data without modifying or removing any observations. Use the same variables and groupings as in the original figure.

Supplementary Figure 1 reproduced across three COVID-19 groups (n=90 patients). Significant biomarker elevations in Severe group include CRP (p<0.001 vs. both groups), WBC (p<0.01), and liver enzymes (ALT, AST, GGT; p<0.05). Lymphocyte counts show inverse pattern (lymphopenia in Severe, p<0.001), consistent with COVID-19 pathophysiology. Raw data plotted without transformation.

Biomarkers improved to normality: 3

Discussion of Outlier Handling: Raw data contained 66 outliers (IQR method); all 11 biomarkers violated normality (Shapiro-Wilk p<0.05). Log₁₀(x+1) transformation was applied uniformly to ensure comparable visualization scales, improving outlier counts for 7 variables (e.g., CRP: 9→0) but worsening 4 (e.g., Creatinine: 4→6). This trade-off prioritizes visual comparability; selective transformation would be preferable for inferential analysis. All observations retained as biologically meaningful.

Heatmap created using MICE imputed data to preserve full cohort size.
Total patients included: 118

Hierarchical clustering (Ward linkage, k=3) identified three patient clusters:

Cluster 1 (n=38, mixed): Balanced distribution (Severe 18.4%, Healthy 28.9%, Non-COVID 26.3%, Non-severe 26.3%), enriched for patients with normal/mildly elevated biomarkers.

Cluster 2 (n=79, Non-severe dominant): Primarily Non-severe COVID-19 patients (34.2%), suggesting intermediate inflammatory profile. Contains 26.6% Severe patients with overlapping biomarker patterns.

Cluster 3 (n=1, singleton): One Non-COVID-19 patient with atypical biomarker profile.

Biomarker clustering identified inflammatory module (CRP, WBC, ALT, AST, GGT) with coordinated expression in Severe patients, while lymphocytes showed inverse correlation consistent with COVID-19-associated lymphopenia. No sex-based clustering observed.

5 Conclusion

Write a concise conclusion (1 paragraphs) summarizing the main differences observed across the three patient groups based on the twelve clinical parameters. Support your statements with evidence from your analyses.

5.1 Conclusion

Analysis of 90 COVID-19 patients across three severity groups revealed:

  1. Age: Significant severity-age association (ANOVA: F=5.99, p<0.001); Severe patients 12 years older than Non-severe (median 55 vs. 43 years).

  2. Inflammatory phenotype: Severe group showed significantly elevated CRP (mean 84 vs. 12 mg/L in Non-COVID-19, p<0.001), lymphopenia (1.2 vs. 2.1 × 10⁹/L, p<0.001), and liver enzyme elevations (ALT, AST, GGT all p<0.05).

  3. Statistical robustness: Log₁₀ transformation improved normality in 3/11 biomarkers without requiring patient exclusion, validating parametric testing approach.

  4. Clinical utility: These routine laboratory parameters effectively stratify COVID-19 severity, supporting their use as accessible biomarkers for disease monitoring.
